summary: A 1975 set of comments on the host and IMP protocol changes proposed in RFC 687. It is updated by RFC 692. See also RFC 696.

eli5.summary: This is someone's feedback on a plan to change how computers and network routers talk, pointing out problems and ideas.

subtitle: Jon Postel annotates a proposed list of Host/IMP protocol changes, point by point.

tldr.problem: RFC 687 proposed changes to the protocol between hosts and their IMPs, and the authors of that plan wanted feedback.
tldr.mechanism: Postel reproduces each point and adds his comment underneath, mostly approving but questioning the field sizes, the packets-per-message control and the host-to-host impact.
tldr.outcome: He calls it a fine set of suggestions, but estimates a lower bound of 48 person-months of system programmer time across the network.

sections.title: What the Comments Cover
sections.content: This memo is a set of comments by Jon Postel on Dave Walden's RFC 687, which suggests changes to the host-IMP protocol. Walden's points are reproduced with Postel's comments underneath. The numbering skips one: the text asks "What happened to 10?".
sections.eli5: Someone wrote a plan, and this is a friend writing short notes under each idea, saying what is good and what looks odd.

sections.title: Leader, Address and Header Fields
sections.content:
The proposal expands the leader from two to five 16-bit words and the address field to 24 bits, made of 16 bits of IMP address and 8 bits of host address. A new optional message length field, 13 bits wide, lets the source host tell the subnetwork the message length in bits. The handling type field grows to eight bits to allow parallel message streams with different handling.

Postel notes that a five-word leader plus the 40-bit host header gives a prefix of 120 bits, not the nice 72-bit boundary of today, unless the host header becomes 64 bits for 144 in total. He concedes the address space is big, at 16,777,216, but prefers an extensible scheme, and suggests a 16-bit length field.
sections.eli5: The plan makes the address label and the envelope bigger. Postel asks whether the new sizes fit neatly and whether the length box should be a bit larger.

sections.title: Other Changes and Compatibility
sections.content:
Further proposals include source control of packets per message, making unordered (type-3) messages a handling type, new fake host addresses without the For/From IMP bit, a parameter on the IMP to host NOP, and a non-blocking host interface. The IMP could refuse a message without blocking, and the host could ask to be told when it may send.

Old and new formats would be supported in parallel, with the host choosing through its host to IMP NOP message. Postel finds this difficult to implement but crucial in an operating environment. He questions the packets-per-message control, since the message length field could be used instead, and approves most of the rest.
sections.eli5: Old and new ways of talking would work side by side for a while, so nobody has to switch overnight.

sections.title: The Cost of the Changes
sections.content:
Postel's overall view is that it is a fine set of suggestions, but he is concerned about the host-to-host protocol changes they imply. His rough guess is a couple of person-months of system programmer time for each operating system on the net.

With 24 systems at 2 person-months each, that is 48 person-months, or 4 person-years, and he says this may be only the lower bound.
sections.eli5: Even a good plan means lots of work for every computer on the network, and he adds up how many months that could take.
